language.script_notes: English signage nationwide; Spanish appears bilingually in the Southwest/border areas. Highway signage uses the FHWA 'Highway Gothic'/Clearview font family, standardized nationwide.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Not commonly used the way Europe uses them; where present, plain reflective posts.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: N/A in most contexts — American roads use painted curbs, delineator posts and guardrails instead of European-style bollards.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Galvanized steel W-beam guardrail is standard nationwide; wooden posts common in National Parks and rural areas painted a medium brown by park convention.
road_furniture.line_paint: Yellow center line (a strong Americas-wide tell vs. most of the world's white), white edge/lane lines. Green highway signs with white text and reflective route shields that vary by state.
road_furniture.curb_style: Poured concrete curbs in developed areas; open roadside ditches common in rural/exurban areas with no curb at all.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Wooden utility poles with cross-arms are the default nationwide (unlike concrete poles common elsewhere); mailbox style (post-mounted rural box vs. house-mounted) and fire hydrant colour/shape vary meaningfully by state/municipality and can help narrow location further.

architecture.roof_style: Asphalt shingle gable and hip roofs dominate residential construction nationwide; low-slope roofs on commercial strip development.
architecture.roof_material: Asphalt shingles are overwhelmingly the default nationwide — a strong general 'this is the US' cue versus tile/slate-dominant countries elsewhere.
architecture.wall_construction: Wood-frame siding construction is the national default (vinyl or wood clapboard siding); brick more common in the Northeast/Midwest, stucco more common in the Southwest/California.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Highly variable by region — muted New England clapboard, red-brick Midwest/Northeast, warm stucco tones in the Southwest.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Strip malls and big-box retail with huge parking lots; wide suburban single-family subdivisions with attached garages; wood-frame houses set back from the road on individual lawns; ubiquitous gas station/fast-food chain signage.

nature.vegetation: Extremely varied by region — see regional profiles for specifics (deciduous Northeast forest, Southern pine, Midwest cropland, Southwest desert, Pacific conifer forest).
nature.terrain: Vast and varied: Appalachian hills in the east, flat interior plains, the Rocky Mountains, desert basins in the Southwest, the Pacific coastal ranges and Sierra Nevada/Cascades in the west.
nature.climate_signature: Ranges from humid subtropical in the Southeast to arid desert in the Southwest to temperate rainforest on the Pacific Northwest coast — no single national climate signature; rely on regional cues.

vehicles.plate_color: Extremely varied by state — each of the 50 states issues its own plate design and colour scheme (e.g. California blue-on-white with yellow accents, New York blue-and-gold, Florida orange with green citrus leaf, Arizona with a purple accent).
vehicles.plate_format: Varies by state: common patterns include ABC-1234, 123-ABC, ABC-123, and 1234AB, among others — state plate design is itself one of the single best in-country location clues.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Full-size pickup trucks (Ford F-series, Chevrolet Silverado, Ram) are disproportionately common versus most other countries — a general US/North America tell alongside yellow school buses.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Full range from Gen 1 through Gen 4. Gen 1 (very low quality, blown-out skies, visible lens-stitching seams) is disproportionately found in the US versus almost anywhere else, making rock-bottom image quality itself a US/Australia/New Zealand tell.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Extremely dense and near-complete across the lower 48 states, including most rural roads; some genuine gaps in remote parts of the Mountain West and Alaska.

confusion_set.shared_traits: English signage, yellow center lines, similar wood-frame suburban architecture and pickup-truck culture near the shared border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Canadian plates are white/blue-and-white with a provincial name, not a US state name; Canadian highway signs use metric (km/h) speeds, and French appears bilingually in Quebec/officially nationwide.

confusion_set.shared_traits: English signage, similar low image quality on older Gen 1 coverage, similar suburban sprawl style
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Australia drives on the LEFT; US drives on the right — this alone settles it once any oncoming traffic or parked cars are visible.

confusion_set.shared_traits: English signage, some shared Gen 1 imagery quality
confusion_set.tiebreaker: New Zealand drives on the LEFT and has no state-by-state license plate variation (one national plate design), unlike the US's wildly varying state plates.
